slides.title: What is money?
slides.text: Money is what we use to buy things. You give money to get what you want.

slides.title: How do you get money?
slides.text: People earn money by working, like doing chores. Feed the dog, and you might earn a coin.

slides.title: Coins and bills
slides.text: Money comes as coins and paper bills. Big or small, it all adds up.

slides.title: What does "spending" mean?
slides.text: Spending means using money to buy something now. You give coins and get a toy back.

slides.title: What is a store?
slides.text: A store is a place that sells things. You give money, and you get to take something home.

slides.title: You can share money too
slides.text: Sometimes people use money to help others. You might buy a gift or give to someone in need.

slides.title: You get to choose!
slides.text: You can save money, spend it, or share it. You get to pick what feels right to you.

slides.title: A job well done
slides.text: Doing a chore is one way to earn money. Clean your room, and you might earn one coin.

slides.title: Money does not grow on trees
slides.text: You cannot just find money everywhere. Someone has to earn it or make it first.

quiz.question: What can you use money for?
choices: Buying things you need
It has no use at all
quiz.explanation: Money buys things like food and toys. You give a coin and get a snack back.

quiz.question: What happens when you use your money to buy a toy?
choices: That's called spending
That's called flying
quiz.explanation: Spending means giving money to get something now, like trading a coin for a toy car.

quiz.question: What is a store?
choices: A place that sells things for money
A place where money grows on trees
quiz.explanation: A store sells things for money. You give coins, and you get to take home a toy.

quiz.question: What are three things you can do with money?
choices: Save it, spend it, or share it
Only ever spend it
quiz.explanation: You can save it in a jar, spend it on a treat, or share it with a friend.

quiz.question: How can you earn money?
choices: By doing a chore, like feeding the dog
By just wishing for it
quiz.explanation: You earn money by doing work, like feeding the dog for a coin.

quiz.question: You clean your room and earn one coin. What did you do to get that coin?
choices: Did a chore
Found it on the ground
quiz.explanation: Cleaning your room is a chore. Doing chores earns coins, like walking a dog earns one too.

quiz.question: What are coins and bills?
choices: Two kinds of money
Two kinds of toys
quiz.explanation: Coins and bills are both money. A shiny coin and a paper dollar can both buy a treat.

quiz.question: If you give a friend some of your money to help them, what are you doing?
choices: Sharing
Losing
quiz.explanation: Sharing means giving some of your money to help someone else, like buying your friend a snack.

quiz.question: True or False: You get to choose what you do with your money.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: True! You can save your coins, spend them on a treat, or share them with someone.

quiz.question: What does a store do?
choices: Sells things for money
Gives away money for free
quiz.explanation: A store sells things for money. Hand over coins, and a toy goes home with you.

slides.title: What does "saving" mean?
slides.text: Saving means you keep money instead of spending it. A piggy bank is a safe place to keep it.

slides.title: Money can grow!
slides.text: Add one coin to your piggy bank each week. Soon your pile of coins gets bigger and bigger.

slides.title: A bank helps too
slides.text: A bank is a safe place for money. It is like a giant piggy bank.

slides.title: Extra money for saving
slides.text: Banks can give you a little extra money. It is a reward just for saving there.

slides.title: Money for now and later
slides.text: Some money is for spending today. Some money is for saving for later.

slides.title: Waiting for something special
slides.text: Some toys cost more money than you have right now. Saving a little each week helps you get it.

slides.title: A goal jar
slides.text: Put a picture of what you want on a jar. Add a coin each day and watch it fill up.

slides.title: Counting your coins
slides.text: Count your coins every week. Watching the number get bigger feels great.

slides.title: Waiting a little longer
slides.text: Sometimes waiting a few weeks helps you get something even better. Patience can pay off.

quiz.question: Where is a safe place to keep money you're saving?
choices: Leave it on the ground
A piggy bank
quiz.explanation: A piggy bank keeps your coins safe until you need them, like a tiny treasure box.

quiz.question: You add one coin every week. What happens to your pile?
choices: It keeps getting bigger
It disappears forever
quiz.explanation: Each coin you add makes your pile bigger, like stacking blocks one on top of another.

quiz.question: A toy costs 10 coins. You only have 4. What can you do?
choices: Save a little each week
Give up on it
quiz.explanation: Saving a few coins each week adds up to 10, like adding 2 coins every week.

quiz.question: What is a bank?
choices: A safe place for your money
A toy store
quiz.explanation: A bank is a safe place that holds your money, like a giant piggy bank for everyone.

quiz.question: What is interest?
choices: Extra money a bank gives you for saving
A fine you have to pay
quiz.explanation: Interest is extra money a bank gives you just for saving there, like a small prize coin.

quiz.question: Which kind of money is for later?
choices: Saving
Spending
quiz.explanation: Saving is money kept for later, like coins tucked away for a toy next month.

quiz.question: What does "saving" mean?
choices: Keeping money instead of spending it
Throwing money away
quiz.explanation: Saving means keeping your coins instead of spending them now, like putting one in a jar.

quiz.question: You want a toy but need more coins. What can help?
choices: Waiting and saving a little more
Giving up right away
quiz.explanation: Waiting and saving a few more coins each week helps you get the toy you want.

quiz.question: Why is it fun to count your saved coins each week?
choices: You can watch your pile grow
It makes the coins disappear
quiz.explanation: Counting your coins each week lets you watch your pile grow, from 3 coins to 4, then 5.

quiz.question: A goal jar helps you...
choices: See how close you are to your goal
Spend all your money right away
quiz.explanation: A goal jar shows how close you are, like a jar that's half full of coins for a new toy.

slides.title: What is a bank?
slides.text: A bank is a safe place where people keep their money, like a giant piggy bank. Instead of hiding coins at home, the bank keeps track of exactly how much is yours.

slides.title: Saving for a goal
slides.text: Instead of spending money right away, you can save it for something bigger that you really want. For example, saving $5 a week toward a $60 bike takes about 12 weeks.

slides.title: What is interest?
slides.text: Some banks pay you a little extra money just for keeping your savings there. That extra bit is called interest, like a small thank-you for saving.

slides.title: Wants vs. needs
slides.text: A need is something you must have, like food or clothes. A want is something nice to have, like a video game.

slides.title: Making a simple budget
slides.text: A budget is a plan for your money, deciding how much to save, spend, and share. For example, $10 could become $5 saved, $3 spent, and $2 shared.

slides.title: Patience pays off
slides.text: Waiting before you buy something often means you can afford something even better later. Spending all $8 today feels fun, but waiting could get you the bigger toy you wanted.

slides.title: Comparing prices
slides.text: Smart shoppers check if the same thing costs less somewhere else before buying it. If a toy costs $12 at one store and $9 at another, checking first saves you $3.

slides.title: Setting a savings goal
slides.text: Picking one thing to save for makes saving feel more real and exciting. Saving $2 a week toward a $16 game takes about 8 weeks.

slides.title: Keeping track of what you spend
slides.text: Writing down what you buy helps you see where your money goes. It's easy to forget that small purchases, like snacks, add up fast.

quiz.question: What is a bank?
choices: A safe place to keep money
A place that takes your money away
quiz.explanation: A bank keeps your money safe, like a giant piggy bank that tracks every dollar. Some banks even pay you extra just for saving there.

quiz.question: If a bank gives you a little extra money just for saving, what's that called?
choices: A fine
Interest
quiz.explanation: Interest is money a bank pays you just for keeping your savings there. If you save $50, the bank might add a little extra on top each year.

quiz.question: Which one is a "need"?
choices: A new video game
Food
quiz.explanation: A need is something you must have to live, like food, water, or clothes. A want, like a new video game, is nice but not required.

quiz.question: A bike costs $60 and you save $5 a week. About how many weeks until you can afford it?
choices: About 12 weeks
It can never be saved for
quiz.explanation: Saving $5 every week adds up: after 12 weeks, you'll have $60 for the bike. Breaking a big goal into small weekly steps makes it easier to reach.

quiz.question: What's it called when you plan out ahead of time how you'll use your money?
choices: A budget
A trophy
quiz.explanation: A budget is a plan for your money before you spend it, deciding how much to save, spend, and share. For example, splitting $10 into $5 saved, $3 spent, and $2 shared.

quiz.question: The same toy costs $12 at one store and $9 at another. Why check both first?
choices: To find the same thing for less
It never makes a difference
quiz.explanation: Comparing prices before buying can save you real money. If the same toy costs $9 instead of $12, checking first puts an extra $3 in your pocket.

quiz.question: What can help make a savings goal feel more real?
choices: Picking one specific thing to save for
Never deciding what you're saving for
quiz.explanation: Picking one specific thing to save for, like a $16 game, gives you something exciting to work toward. A clear target makes it easier to stick with saving.

quiz.question: What's the difference between a "want" and a "need"?
choices: A need is required, a want is nice to have
They mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: A need is something you must have, like food or a coat in winter. A want, like a new toy, is nice to have but not necessary.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to write down what you spend?
choices: It helps you see where your money is going
It makes your money disappear
quiz.explanation: Writing down what you buy shows exactly where your money goes each week. Small purchases, like a $2 snack a few times, can quietly add up to a lot.

quiz.question: You wait two weeks instead of buying a toy right away, and end up affording a better one. What does that show?
choices: Patience can pay off
Waiting never helps
quiz.explanation: Waiting before buying gives you time to save more and sometimes afford something better. Skipping a small toy today could mean a bigger one in just a couple of weeks.

slides.title: What is a bank account?
slides.text: A bank account is like a digital piggy bank that tracks exactly how much money you have. Instead of counting coins, a bank statement might just say balance: $37.

slides.title: Watching your savings add up
slides.text: Writing down how much you save each week helps you see your money growing. A simple chart like $2, $4, $6, $8 turns saving into something you can watch happen.

slides.title: Risk and reward
slides.text: Putting money into something new means it could grow, but it could also lose value. Taking a small risk is part of how your money can earn more over time.

slides.title: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
slides.text: Spreading your money across a few different things is called diversifying. If one thing does poorly, the others can help make up for it.

slides.title: Saving vs. growing your money
slides.text: Saving keeps your money the same amount, safe and ready to use. Investing is different — it puts your money to work, hoping it grows into more.

slides.title: Interest can earn more interest
slides.text: When your saved interest stays in the bank, it can earn its own interest too. That's called compound growth, and it helps your money grow faster over time.

slides.title: What is a stock, simply?
slides.text: A stock is a tiny piece of a company that you can own. If the company does well, your tiny piece can be worth more.

slides.title: Companies you know
slides.text: Companies that make your favorite shoes, games, or snacks sell tiny pieces of themselves called stocks. People buy those pieces hoping the company grows.

slides.title: Why starting young helps
slides.text: The earlier you start saving or investing, even a little, the more time your money has to grow. A few dollars started at age 8 has many years to grow before you're all grown up.

slides.title: Ups and downs are normal
slides.text: An investment's value can go up some days and down on others, kind of like a rollercoaster. Riding it out instead of panicking usually works out better.

quiz.question: What is a bank account?
choices: A way the bank keeps track of exactly how much money you have
A type of toy
quiz.explanation: A bank account is like a digital piggy bank that keeps track of your exact balance. Instead of counting coins, you just check a number, like balance: $37.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to write down and add up your savings each week?
choices: You can actually see your money growing toward your goal
It has no real purpose
quiz.explanation: Writing down your savings each week lets you actually watch the total climb, like $2, then $4, then $6. Seeing the numbers grow keeps you motivated to keep going.

quiz.question: What happens when you take a risk with your money?
choices: It could grow, but it could also lose value
Nothing ever changes
quiz.explanation: Taking a risk with money means it could grow bigger, but it could also shrink for a while. That up-and-down chance is part of how investing can earn more over time.

quiz.question: What does it mean to diversify your money?
choices: Spread it across a few different things
Put it all in one place
quiz.explanation: Diversifying means putting your money into a few different things instead of just one. If one investment does poorly, the others can help balance it out.

quiz.question: What is compound growth?
choices: When your interest earns its own interest too
When a bank charges you a fee
quiz.explanation: Compound growth happens when the interest you already earned starts earning its own interest too. Money left in the bank grows a little faster each year instead of staying flat.

quiz.question: What is a stock?
choices: A tiny piece of a company you can own
A type of bank account
quiz.explanation: A stock is a tiny piece of a real company that you can own. If that company sells more toys or games, your tiny piece can become worth more.

quiz.question: If a company you own a small piece of grows and does well, what usually happens?
choices: Your piece becomes worth more
Your piece disappears
quiz.explanation: When a company does well and earns more money, the small pieces people own often become worth more too. Your slice of the company grows in value right along with it.

quiz.question: Why does starting to save or invest young help so much?
choices: Your money has more time to grow
It doesn't make any difference
quiz.explanation: Starting to save or invest young gives your money many more years to grow. A few dollars saved at age 8 has far more time to add up than money started at 20.

quiz.question: An investment goes up some weeks and down other weeks. Is that normal?
choices: Yes, that's a normal part of investing
No, real investments never change
quiz.explanation: Yes, an investment's value naturally goes up some weeks and down others, like a rollercoaster ride. Staying patient through the dips instead of panicking usually works out better in the end.

quiz.question: What's the main difference between saving and investing?
choices: Saving keeps your money the same; investing tries to grow it
They are exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: Saving keeps your money the exact same amount and safe, ready whenever you need it. Investing puts your money to work instead, hoping it grows into more than you started with.

slides.title: What is investing?
slides.text: Investing means using your money to buy a small piece of something — like a company — hoping it grows in value over time. For example, if you use $50 to buy a small piece of a company that makes sneakers, and more people start buying those sneakers, your $50 piece could grow to be worth $60 or more.

slides.title: What is a stock?
slides.text: A stock is a tiny piece of ownership in a company. If the company does well, your tiny piece can become worth more. For example, if a company that makes your favorite video game has 1,000 total pieces (stocks) and you own 1 of them, you technically own a tiny 1/1000th sliver of that whole company.

slides.title: Risk and reward
slides.text: Investments can go up AND down in value. Taking on some risk is part of how investing can lead to bigger rewards over time. For example, $100 invested might grow to $110 in a good year, but it could also drop to $90 in a rough year before recovering later — that up-and-down ride is the risk part of the deal.

slides.title: What is a "loss"?
slides.text: Sometimes an investment's value drops for a while — that's a loss on paper. It only becomes a real loss if you sell while it's down instead of waiting for it to recover. For example, if your $100 investment drops to $80 but you leave it alone and it climbs back to $105 a year later, you never actually lost anything — the dip was only temporary.

slides.title: Investing vs. an allowance
slides.text: An allowance is money you're simply given. Investing is different — it's money you put to work, hoping it grows into more than you started with. For example, a $10 weekly allowance stays $10 no matter what, but $10 invested wisely could grow to be worth $12, $15, or more over several years.

slides.title: What is a company, really?
slides.text: A company is a business that makes or sells something, like sneakers, games, or snacks. When you buy a stock, you're buying a tiny slice of that actual business, not just a picture of it.

slides.title: Investors: everyday people, not just experts
slides.text: You don't need to be a grown-up genius to invest. Millions of everyday people, including teenagers with a parent's help, own small pieces of companies through simple accounts.

slides.title: Why would a company's stock go up?
slides.text: If more people want to buy what a company sells, the company usually earns more money, and its stock often becomes more valuable. For example, if a sneaker company sells way more shoes this year than last year, its stock price often climbs.

slides.title: Investing is not gambling
slides.text: Gambling is mostly luck with no real strategy behind it. Investing means owning a real part of a real business, and long-term investors research and think through their choices instead of just guessing.

quiz.question: What does "investing" mean?
choices: Using money to buy something that can grow in value
Hiding money so nobody can find it
quiz.explanation: Investing means putting your money into something, like a small piece of a company, instead of just spending it. If that company grows, like a sneaker brand selling more shoes, your $50 piece could grow to $60 or more over time.

quiz.question: What is a stock?
choices: A type of bank account
A small piece of ownership in a company
quiz.explanation: A stock is a small piece of ownership in a real company, not just a fake certificate. If a video game company splits itself into 1,000 stocks and you own 1, you technically own 1/1000th of that whole business.

quiz.question: True or False: Investments only ever go up in value.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: False — investments can go up and down in value, not just rise forever. For example, $100 might grow to $110 in a good year but dip to $90 in a rough one before recovering; that ride is the risk that makes bigger rewards possible.

quiz.question: If a company you own a tiny piece of grows and does well, what usually happens to your piece?
choices: It becomes worth more
It disappears
quiz.explanation: When a company grows and earns more money, the small pieces of it that people own — including yours — usually become worth more too. It's like owning a slice of a pizza that keeps getting bigger.

quiz.question: An investment drops in value for a while, but you leave it alone and it recovers later. Was that a real loss?
choices: No — it only becomes a real loss if you sell while it's down
Yes, any drop is a permanent loss
quiz.explanation: No — a drop in value is only a loss "on paper" until you actually sell. If your $100 investment falls to $80 but you wait and it climbs back to $105 a year later, you never really lost anything at all.

quiz.question: When you buy a stock, what are you actually buying?
choices: A tiny slice of a real company
A gift card to a store
quiz.explanation: When you buy a stock, you're buying a tiny slice of an actual, real business — not just a picture or a promise. Owning shares in a snack company, for example, means you truly own a small part of that company.

quiz.question: Can everyday people, not just experts, own stocks?
choices: Yes, including teens with a parent's help
No, only professional traders can
quiz.explanation: Yes — millions of ordinary people, including teenagers with a parent's help, own small pieces of companies through simple accounts. You don't need to be a finance expert or a grown-up genius to start investing.

quiz.question: A sneaker company sells way more shoes than last year. What might happen to its stock?
choices: It could become more valuable
It always stays exactly the same
quiz.explanation: When a company sells a lot more of its product, like shoes, it usually earns more money as a result. Investors often notice, which makes the company's stock become more valuable, since more people want to own a piece of it.

quiz.question: What's a key difference between investing and gambling?
choices: Investing means owning a real part of a business, unlike a guess-based bet
There is no difference at all
quiz.explanation: Gambling is mostly luck, with no real strategy or research behind the bet. Investing means actually owning a real part of a real business, and long-term investors study a company's numbers and plans instead of just guessing.

quiz.question: Why do risk and reward usually go together in investing?
choices: Taking on some risk is part of how money can grow more over time
Taking risks never has any effect on growth
quiz.explanation: Risk and reward go together because taking on some chance of loss is part of what allows money to grow faster than it would sitting still. A savings account barely grows, but accepting some risk, like owning stock, opens the door to bigger gains over years.

slides.title: The power of time
slides.text: The earlier you start investing — even with a small amount — the more time your money has to grow. Time is a young investor's biggest advantage. For example, $100 invested at age 12 has decades to grow before retirement, while the same $100 invested at age 40 has far less time to do the same job.

slides.title: What is compound interest?
slides.text: Compound interest means you earn money not just on what you put in, but also on the money it already earned before. It's growth building on growth. For example, $100 growing by 10% becomes $110 after year one — then in year two, that 10% growth applies to the full $110, not just your original $100, making $121.

slides.title: Short-term vs. long-term goals
slides.text: Money you need soon (like next month) is usually better off saved, not invested. Money you won't need for many years has more room to ride out an investment's ups and downs. For example, money for a video game you want to buy next month should stay in simple savings, while money you won't touch for 5+ years has time to recover from any dips.

slides.title: Investing a little, regularly
slides.text: Instead of investing one big amount all at once, some people invest a smaller amount on a regular schedule — like monthly. This is sometimes called dollar-cost averaging, and it smooths out the ups and downs. For example, investing $10 every month for a year means some months you buy when prices are higher and some when they're lower, which balances out instead of betting everything on one moment.

slides.title: Compounding, one more year
slides.text: Compound growth keeps building on itself each year. $200 growing at 8% becomes $216 after year one, then $233.28 after year two, because the 8% now applies to $216, not just the original $200.

slides.title: Small amounts, big results
slides.text: Investing just $5 a week doesn't sound like much, but it adds up to $260 in a year. Left to grow for years, small regular amounts can turn into a surprisingly large total.

slides.title: Starting at 11 vs. starting at 25
slides.text: $500 invested at age 11 has roughly 50+ years to grow before retirement age, while the same $500 invested at 25 has around 15 fewer years to do the same job. Those extra years matter enormously.

slides.title: Matching your goal to your timeline
slides.text: A goal that's just months away, like a new phone, should usually stay in simple savings. A goal that's many years away, like a car at 16 or college, has time to ride out investing's ups and downs.

slides.title: Why regular investing smooths the ride
slides.text: Investing the same amount every month means you naturally buy more when prices are low and less when prices are high, averaging out over time instead of guessing when's best.

quiz.question: Why is starting young such a big advantage for investing?
choices: More time for your money to grow
It isn't actually an advantage
quiz.explanation: Starting young matters because time lets compound growth do its work, turning small amounts into much larger ones. $100 invested at age 12 has decades to grow before retirement, far more than the same $100 invested at 40.

quiz.question: $100 growing 10% becomes $110. Why does year two's 10% growth apply to $110, not $100?
choices: Because that's compound interest — growth building on top of previous growth
Because banks round numbers up randomly
quiz.explanation: This is compound interest — each year's growth is calculated on your new, bigger total, not just your starting amount. After year one, $100 becomes $110; in year two, the 10% growth applies to the full $110, making $121.

quiz.question: What is "dollar-cost averaging"?
choices: Investing a smaller amount regularly instead of all at once
Only ever investing in dollar bills
quiz.explanation: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a smaller, steady amount on a regular schedule, like $10 every month, instead of one big lump sum. This way, you naturally buy at both high and low prices, which smooths out the ride.

quiz.question: $200 grows at 8% a year. Why does year two's growth apply to $216, not $200?
choices: Because compounding builds on the new, larger total each year
Because banks add a random bonus each year
quiz.explanation: Compounding means each year's growth is calculated on the total you have so far, including previous growth. $200 becomes $216 after year one, and in year two the 8% growth applies to that bigger $216, not the original $200.

quiz.question: Investing $5 a week for a year adds up to about how much?
choices: About $260
About $26
quiz.explanation: $5 a week for 52 weeks adds up to about $260 — small, steady amounts build into a real total surprisingly fast. Left to grow for years afterward, that pattern can turn into an even bigger sum.

quiz.question: $500 invested at age 11 vs the same $500 invested at age 25 — which has more time to grow before retirement?
choices: The $500 invested at age 11
They have exactly the same amount of time
quiz.explanation: Money invested at age 11 has roughly 15 more years to grow before retirement than the same money invested at 25. Those extra years matter enormously, since compound growth speeds up the longer it runs.

quiz.question: You want to buy a new phone in 3 months. Where should that money likely stay?
choices: In simple savings, not invested
Invested, since more time always helps
quiz.explanation: Money you'll need soon, like in 3 months for a phone, should stay in simple savings rather than invested. Investments can dip in value for a while, and a short-term dip could mean you don't have enough when you need it.

quiz.question: Why might investing the same amount every month help smooth out ups and downs?
choices: You end up buying more when prices are low and less when high
It guarantees prices never change
quiz.explanation: Investing the same amount every month means you automatically buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high. Over time, this averages out your cost instead of you having to guess the perfect moment to buy.

quiz.question: What is the biggest advantage a young investor typically has?
choices: Time for their money to compound
A bigger allowance than adults
quiz.explanation: The biggest advantage a young investor has is time, because compound growth needs years to really build momentum. Even a small amount invested early can end up bigger than a larger amount invested later, simply because it had more time.

quiz.question: True or False: A goal that's many years away can usually handle more investing ups and downs than a goal that's just weeks away.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: True — a goal that's many years away gives an investment plenty of time to recover from a dip before you need the money. A goal just weeks away doesn't have that cushion, so it's safer kept in savings instead.

slides.title: What is a brokerage account?
slides.text: A brokerage account is where you actually buy and hold investments like stocks — different from a regular bank account, which just holds cash. For example, a parent might open a custodial brokerage account for a young teen, where the teen can pick which companies to invest small amounts in, with a parent supervising.

slides.title: Diversification: spreading it out
slides.text: Diversification means putting your money into many different investments instead of just one, so a single bad outcome doesn't hurt you too much. For example, if you invest $100 in 10 different companies instead of just 1, one company doing badly only affects a small slice of your total money instead of all of it.

slides.title: Why prices go up over time
slides.text: Prices for things like candy or games tend to rise a little every year — this is called inflation. For example, if a $1 snack rises in price by about 3% each year, it could cost around $1.16 after five years, so money that just sits still slowly buys less.

slides.title: What is an index fund?
slides.text: An index fund is a single investment that gives you a tiny slice of many companies at once, instead of picking just one. For example, buying one index fund might give you a small piece of 500 different companies, so you don't have to research and buy each one yourself.

slides.title: Fees can eat into your growth
slides.text: Some investments charge a small fee every year just for holding them, which quietly reduces how much you earn. For example, a $100 investment charging a 1% yearly fee costs you about $1 a year, which may not sound like much but adds up over many years.

slides.title: Custodial accounts, explained
slides.text: A custodial account is a brokerage account a parent opens and manages for a kid, until the kid becomes an adult. It lets a young person actually own real investments earlier than they otherwise could.

slides.title: Researching before you invest
slides.text: Before buying a stock, smart investors look into what the company does, how it's been doing, and whether they believe in its future. A little research helps you invest with reasons, not just guesses.

slides.title: Cash loses value slowly
slides.text: Money kept as plain cash under a mattress doesn't earn anything, so inflation quietly shrinks what it can buy each year. Investing is one way to try to grow money faster than inflation shrinks it.

slides.title: Reading a simple account statement
slides.text: A brokerage statement might show you own 3 shares of a $40 stock, worth $120 total. Checking it now and then helps you see how your investments are actually doing.

quiz.question: What is a brokerage account used for?
choices: Actually buying and holding investments like stocks
Only storing cash, like a regular bank account
quiz.explanation: A brokerage account is specifically where you buy and hold investments like stocks, unlike a regular bank account that just holds cash. A parent might open one for a teen so they can pick companies to invest small amounts in, with supervision.

quiz.question: What does diversification mean?
choices: Spreading your money across many investments
Putting all your money in one company
quiz.explanation: Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments instead of putting it all into one. If you invest $100 across 10 companies instead of 1, one company doing badly only affects a small slice of your total money.

quiz.question: What is inflation?
choices: Prices slowly rising over time
Prices always staying exactly the same
quiz.explanation: Inflation is prices slowly rising over time, which means money that just sits still buys a little less each year. A $1 snack rising 3% a year could cost about $1.16 after five years.

quiz.question: What is an index fund?
choices: A single investment that owns tiny pieces of many companies
A type of piggy bank
quiz.explanation: An index fund is a single investment that gives you a tiny slice of many companies at once, instead of you picking just one. Buying one index fund might give you a small piece of 500 different companies without having to research each one yourself.

quiz.question: What is a custodial account?
choices: A brokerage account a parent manages for a kid until they're an adult
A type of savings piggy bank
quiz.explanation: A custodial account is a brokerage account that a parent opens and manages for a kid until they become an adult. It lets a young person actually own real investments earlier than they otherwise could on their own.

quiz.question: Why do smart investors research a company before buying its stock?
choices: So they invest with real reasons instead of just guessing
Research never actually helps
quiz.explanation: Researching a company before buying its stock means looking into what it does, how it's been performing, and whether you believe in its future. This helps you invest with real reasons behind your choice instead of just guessing.

quiz.question: Why does keeping money as plain cash slowly lose value?
choices: Because inflation makes prices rise while the cash stays the same
Because cash actually shrinks in size over time
quiz.explanation: Cash kept under a mattress doesn't earn anything, but prices around it keep rising due to inflation. That means the same amount of cash buys a little less each year, even though the number of dollars never changes.

quiz.question: A statement shows you own 3 shares worth $40 each. What's your total value?
quiz.explanation: Three shares worth $40 each add up to a total of $120, since you multiply the number of shares by the price of each one. Checking a statement like this shows you exactly what your investments are worth right now.

quiz.question: What does a $100 investment charging a 1% yearly fee cost you in fees that year?
choices: About $1
About $100
quiz.explanation: A 1% yearly fee on a $100 investment costs about $1 that year, since 1% of 100 is 1. It sounds tiny, but fees like this are charged every year and can add up to a real amount over many years.

quiz.question: Why might an index fund be easier for a beginner than picking individual stocks?
choices: It automatically spreads your money across many companies at once
It only ever invests in one company
quiz.explanation: An index fund is easier for a beginner because it automatically spreads your money across many companies in one purchase. Instead of researching and buying 500 individual stocks yourself, one index fund purchase does that spreading for you.

slides.title: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
slides.text: Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments instead of just one, so a single bad investment doesn't sink your whole total. For example, putting $500 into 100 different companies means one company struggling barely affects your overall money, unlike putting all $500 into just one.

slides.title: What is an index fund?
slides.text: An index fund is a single investment that gives you a small stake in hundreds of companies at once, making it an easy way to diversify. For example, one index fund purchase might give you a tiny piece of the 500 largest companies in the country, instead of you having to research and buy 500 stocks yourself.

slides.title: The Rule of 72
slides.text: The Rule of 72 is a quick trick to estimate how many years it takes your money to double: just divide 72 by your yearly growth rate. For example, $500 growing at 8% a year would roughly double to $1,000 in about 9 years, since 72 ÷ 8 = 9.

slides.title: What is a bull market?
slides.text: A bull market is a stretch of time when stock prices are generally rising. Bull markets can last for years and are a completely normal part of a long investing journey.

slides.title: What is a bear market?
slides.text: A bear market is a stretch of time when stock prices are generally falling. Bear markets feel scary in the moment, but investors who stay patient through them have historically come out ahead later.

slides.title: Compound growth: earning on your earnings
slides.text: Compound growth means your investment earns money on both what you put in and on the money it already earned. For example, $1,000 growing 7% a year becomes $1,070 after year one, then grows from that bigger $1,070 the next year instead of from the original $1,000.

slides.title: Stocks vs. bonds, simply
slides.text: A stock is a tiny ownership slice of a company; a bond is more like a loan you give a company or government, which pays you back with interest. Owning a $1,000 bond might pay you $30 a year until the company repays your original $1,000.

slides.title: Building a simple portfolio
slides.text: A portfolio is just the whole collection of investments someone owns, like a folder holding several types of investments instead of one. Someone might hold 70% in a stock index fund and 30% in bonds, mixing growth with steadier stability.

slides.title: Volatility, defined
slides.text: Volatility means how much an investment's price jumps around in the short term. A stock that swings between $80 and $120 in a month is more volatile than one that barely moves from $95 to $100.

quiz.question: What does "diversification" mean?
choices: Putting all your money into one company
Spreading your money across many different investments
quiz.explanation: Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments instead of concentrating it in one. Putting $500 into 100 different companies means one company struggling barely dents your overall total, unlike putting the full $500 into just one company.

quiz.question: What is an index fund?
choices: A fund that owns tiny pieces of hundreds of companies at once
A savings account with no interest
quiz.explanation: An index fund is a single investment that gives you a small stake in hundreds of companies at once, making it an easy way to diversify. One purchase might give you a tiny piece of the 500 largest companies in the country instead of researching each one yourself.

quiz.question: Using the Rule of 72, about how many years would it take money to double at 9% yearly growth?
choices: About 8 years
About 50 years
quiz.explanation: The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly growth rate. At 9% growth, 72 divided by 9 equals 8, so money roughly doubles in about 8 years.

quiz.question: What is a "bear market"?
choices: A stretch of time when prices are generally falling
A market that only sells stuffed animals
quiz.explanation: A bear market is a stretch of time when stock prices are generally falling, sometimes for months or longer. It's a normal, if uncomfortable, part of investing — history shows markets have always eventually recovered and moved on to new highs.

quiz.question: What is compound growth?
choices: Earning money on both what you put in and on money already earned
Only earning money once at the very end
quiz.explanation: Compound growth means an investment earns money on both what you originally put in and on the money it already earned. $1,000 growing 7% a year becomes $1,070 after year one, and the next year's growth is calculated on that larger $1,070, not the original $1,000.

quiz.question: What's the main difference between a stock and a bond?
choices: A stock is ownership in a company; a bond is more like a loan to it
They are exactly the same investment
quiz.explanation: A stock makes you a part-owner of a company, while a bond is more like a loan you give a company or government in exchange for interest payments. Owning a $1,000 bond might pay you $30 a year until the borrower eventually repays your original $1,000.

quiz.question: What is a portfolio?
choices: The whole collection of investments someone owns
A single type of stock only
quiz.explanation: A portfolio is simply the whole collection of investments someone owns, like a folder holding several different pieces instead of just one. Someone might hold 70% in a stock index fund and 30% in bonds, blending growth potential with steadier stability.

quiz.question: A stock swings between $80 and $120 in a month. What term describes that kind of price swinging?
choices: Volatility
Inflation
quiz.explanation: Volatility describes how much an investment's price swings around in the short term. A stock bouncing between $80 and $120 in a single month is far more volatile than one that barely moves from $95 to $100 over the same time.

quiz.question: What is a bull market?
choices: A stretch of time when prices are generally rising
A market that only trades farm animals
quiz.explanation: A bull market is a stretch of time when stock prices are generally rising, sometimes lasting for years at a stretch. It's the flip side of a bear market, and long-term investors typically experience both kinds of stretches many times over their lives.

quiz.question: Why might someone mix stocks and bonds in a portfolio?
choices: To blend growth potential with steadier stability
Because it's required by law
quiz.explanation: Mixing stocks and bonds in a portfolio blends the higher growth potential of stocks with the steadier, more predictable payments of bonds. This balance can smooth out the overall ride, since bonds tend to hold up better when stock prices are falling.

slides.title: Inflation: the silent thief
slides.text: Prices tend to rise over time, so money that just sits still slowly loses buying power — that rise in prices is called inflation. For example, if a candy bar costs $1 today and prices rise 3% a year, it could cost about $1.34 in ten years, meaning $100 in cash quietly buys less and less.

slides.title: Long-term thinking beats quick wins
slides.text: Investors who stay patient through ups and downs, over years or decades, tend to do far better than those chasing quick trades. For example, someone who invested $1,000 and left it alone for 20 years, riding out several rough patches, has historically ended up far ahead of someone who panic-sold every time prices dipped.

slides.title: Debt works the opposite way
slides.text: Investing grows money for you over time, but borrowing money — debt — usually costs you extra through interest, working against you instead of for you. For example, a $200 credit card balance charging 20% interest a year can balloon if left unpaid, the same way compound growth builds up an investment, just in the wrong direction.

slides.title: Retirement accounts, simplified
slides.text: A retirement account is a special account for investing money you won't touch for decades, often with tax benefits along the way. For example, some employers add extra money when you contribute — put in $50, and your employer might add another $25 for free, instantly growing your investment.

slides.title: Why an emergency fund matters
slides.text: An emergency fund is cash set aside for surprises, like a car repair, that you can reach without selling your investments. For example, keeping a few months of expenses in easy-to-reach savings means a sudden bill doesn't force you to sell investments at a bad time.

slides.title: Good debt vs. bad debt
slides.text: Not all debt is equally bad — a loan for something that can increase your future earning power, like education, is often viewed differently than debt for things that lose value fast. Even so, any debt costs extra through interest, so borrowing less is almost always safer.

slides.title: Building an emergency fund, step by step
slides.text: A common target is 3 to 6 months of expenses set aside in easy-to-reach savings. Someone who spends $500 a month might aim to save $1,500 to $3,000 before investing aggressively.

slides.title: What a real downturn feels like
slides.text: During a rough stretch, an investment worth $1,000 might drop to $700 before recovering over the following year or two. Investors who sell in a panic lock in that loss, while those who wait it out often see the value come back.

slides.title: Time horizon shapes your choices
slides.text: Time horizon just means how long until you'll need the money. Someone investing for a goal 15 years away can usually handle a bigger dip than someone who needs the money in six months.

quiz.question: A candy bar costs $1 today. If prices rise 3% a year, what happens to its price over 10 years?
choices: It rises to roughly $1.34, since prices rising over time is inflation
It always stays exactly $1
quiz.explanation: Prices rising over time is called inflation, and it means money that just sits still slowly loses buying power. A $1 candy bar rising 3% a year would cost roughly $1.34 after ten years, so the same dollar buys noticeably less.

quiz.question: True or False: Reacting quickly to every market dip usually leads to better long-term results.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: False — reacting to every dip by selling in a panic usually hurts long-term results more than it helps. Investors who stay patient through ups and downs over years or decades have historically ended up far ahead of those chasing quick moves.

quiz.question: A $200 credit card balance at 20% interest grows if unpaid. Why is this the "opposite" of investing?
choices: Because compounding is working against you instead of for you
Because credit cards use a completely different kind of math
quiz.explanation: A $200 credit card balance charging 20% interest can balloon if left unpaid, because interest compounds on top of interest, the same mechanism that grows investments — just working in the wrong direction. Debt grows against you while investing aims to grow money for you.

quiz.question: What is an emergency fund for?
choices: Cash you can use for surprises without selling your investments
Money you're never allowed to touch
quiz.explanation: An emergency fund is cash set aside for surprises, like a car repair, that you can reach without selling your investments. Keeping a few months of expenses in easy-to-reach savings means a sudden bill doesn't force you to sell at a bad time.

quiz.question: Why might a loan for education be viewed differently from debt for something that loses value fast?
choices: It can increase future earning power, though it still costs interest
Because it never has to be paid back
quiz.explanation: A loan for education is often viewed differently from debt for something that loses value fast, because it can increase your future earning power. Even so, it still costs extra through interest, so borrowing less is almost always the safer choice.

quiz.question: Someone spends $500 a month. Using a 3-to-6-month target, about how much might their emergency fund aim to hold?
quiz.explanation: A common emergency fund target is 3 to 6 months of expenses kept in easy-to-reach savings. Someone spending $500 a month would multiply that out to aim for somewhere between $1,500 and $3,000 before investing more aggressively.

quiz.question: An investment drops from $1,000 to $700, then recovers to $1,050 a year later. Who "locks in" the loss?
choices: Someone who panics and sells while it's at $700
Someone who waits it out
quiz.explanation: Someone who panics and sells while the investment is down at $700 locks in that loss permanently, turning a temporary dip into a real one. Someone who waits it out gets to keep the eventual recovery, ending up with $1,050 instead.

quiz.question: What does "time horizon" mean?
choices: How long until you'll actually need the money
How much money you currently have
quiz.explanation: Time horizon means how long until you'll actually need the money you've invested. Someone investing for a goal 15 years away can usually handle a much bigger dip than someone who needs the money in just six months.

quiz.question: Someone investing for a goal 15 years away can usually handle bigger dips than someone needing the money in 6 months. Why?
choices: They have much more time to wait out a recovery
Time horizon has no effect on risk
quiz.explanation: A longer time horizon gives an investment far more time to recover from a downturn before the money is actually needed. Someone with 15 years to go can simply wait out a rough stretch, while someone needing cash in 6 months can't afford to wait.

quiz.question: What is a retirement account generally used for?
choices: Investing money you won't touch for decades, often with tax benefits
Spending money the same week you earn it
quiz.explanation: A retirement account is built for investing money you won't touch for decades, often with tax benefits that help it grow faster. Some employers even add extra money when you contribute, like adding $25 for free when you put in $50.

slides.title: Getting started today
slides.text: Modern investing apps and custodial accounts have made it easier than ever for a teenager to start investing small, real amounts with a parent's help. For example, a 16-year-old could start with just $20 in a custodial brokerage account, buying a small stake in an index fund and adding a bit more each month.

slides.title: A brief word on taxes
slides.text: In many places, profit made from selling an investment can be taxed — often called a capital gains tax. For example, if you bought a stock for $100 and sold it for $150, that $50 profit might be taxed, so your actual take-home gain would be a bit less than $50.

slides.title: Fees quietly add up
slides.text: An expense ratio is a small yearly fee some investments charge just for holding them. For example, a $10,000 investment with a 1% expense ratio costs about $100 a year, which can add up to thousands of dollars over a few decades.

slides.title: Risk tolerance and time horizon
slides.text: Risk tolerance is how comfortable you are watching your investment's value swing up and down. For example, someone investing money they won't need for 20 years can usually handle bigger swings than someone who needs the money in just one year.

slides.title: What a custodial brokerage account is
slides.text: A custodial brokerage account is opened and legally controlled by a parent, but the investments inside it belong to the teen. At a set age, often 18 or 21 depending on the state, control transfers fully to them.

slides.title: Why keeping records matters
slides.text: Every time you sell an investment for a profit, you may owe tax on that profit, so keeping simple records of what you paid and what you sold it for makes filing much easier later. A quick note of dates and prices saves a lot of hassle.

slides.title: Comparing two funds by their fees
slides.text: Fund A charges a 0.05% yearly fee, Fund B charges 1%. On a $5,000 investment, that's a $2.50 fee for Fund A versus $50 for Fund B in a single year, a gap that grows much larger over decades.

slides.title: Picking investments that match your goals
slides.text: Someone saving for a house in 5 years might choose steadier investments, while someone investing for retirement in 40 years can typically afford to take on more ups and downs. There's no single right portfolio for everyone.

slides.title: Why you shouldn't invest money you need soon
slides.text: Money you'll need within the next year or two should generally stay out of investments that can drop in value. That way, a bad month in the market never forces you to sell at a loss just to pay a bill.

quiz.question: What's one key benefit of starting to invest as a teenager instead of waiting until your 30s?
choices: Many more years for compound growth
No real benefit either way
quiz.explanation: Starting to invest as a teenager instead of waiting until your 30s gives your money many more years for compound growth to work. A small amount invested at 16 has decades longer to grow than the same amount invested at 32, even without adding more.

quiz.question: You buy a stock for $100 and sell it for $150. What might a capital gains tax apply to?
choices: The $50 profit you made
The full $150 you received
quiz.explanation: A capital gains tax typically applies only to the profit made from selling an investment, not the full amount received. If you bought a stock for $100 and sold it for $150, the tax would generally apply to the $50 profit, not the whole $150.

quiz.question: What is an expense ratio?
choices: A small yearly fee some investments charge
A tax on all your income
quiz.explanation: An expense ratio is a small yearly fee some investments charge just for holding them, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A $10,000 investment with a 1% expense ratio costs about $100 a year, which can add up to thousands over a few decades.

quiz.question: In a custodial brokerage account, who legally controls it until the teen reaches a set age?
choices: A parent
A random stranger
quiz.explanation: A parent legally controls a custodial brokerage account, even though the investments inside it actually belong to the teen. At a set age, often 18 or 21 depending on the state, full control transfers over to the teen.

quiz.question: Why is it smart to keep simple records of what you paid and sold an investment for?
choices: It makes figuring out any tax owed on the profit much easier
Records are never actually needed
quiz.explanation: Keeping simple records of what you paid for an investment and what you sold it for makes it far easier to figure out any tax owed on the profit. A quick note of dates and prices at the time saves a lot of hassle later on.

quiz.question: Fund A charges 0.05% a year and Fund B charges 1%. On a $5,000 investment, roughly what's the fee gap in one year?
choices: About $47.50 more for Fund B
There is no real difference
quiz.explanation: Fund A's 0.05% fee costs about $2.50 a year on $5,000, while Fund B's 1% fee costs about $50, a gap of roughly $47.50 in just that one year. Over decades, small fee differences like this compound into a much larger gap.

quiz.question: Why might someone saving for a house in 5 years choose steadier investments than someone saving for retirement in 40 years?
choices: They have less time to recover from a big dip
Steadier investments are always required by law
quiz.explanation: Someone saving for a house in 5 years has much less time to recover from a big dip than someone investing for retirement 40 years away. A shorter time horizon leaves less room to ride out a downturn before the money is actually needed.

quiz.question: Why is it risky to invest money you'll need within the next year or two?
choices: A bad month could force you to sell at a loss to cover a bill
Investing that money always guarantees a profit
quiz.explanation: Investing money you'll need within the next year or two is risky because a bad month in the market could force you to sell at a loss just to cover a bill. Keeping short-term money out of investments protects it from that kind of bad timing.

quiz.question: What does risk tolerance mean?
choices: How comfortable you are watching your investment's value swing up and down
How much money you're required to invest
quiz.explanation: Risk tolerance describes how comfortable you are watching your investment's value swing up and down without panicking and selling. Someone investing money they won't need for 20 years can usually handle bigger swings than someone who needs the money in just one year.

quiz.question: What's one benefit modern investing apps and custodial accounts give a teenager?
choices: An easier way to start investing small, real amounts with a parent's help
Guaranteed profits with no risk at all
quiz.explanation: Modern investing apps and custodial accounts make it far easier for a teenager to start investing small, real amounts with a parent's help. A 16-year-old could begin with just $20 in an index fund and add a bit more each month from there.
